overlap.title: The collection prescribes several kinds of sanctions
overlap.summary: Death, being cut off and childlessness are described separately rather than as one uniform penalty.
overlap.reasoning: The wording distinguishes sanctions. The meaning and administration of being cut off cannot simply be assumed identical to every explicit execution command.
overlap.scope: This records the ancient prescriptions without endorsing them. It does not establish actual enforcement or a biological cause of childlessness; historical interpretation and ethical evaluation remain separate tasks.

overlap.title: Saul “enquired of the LORD”, and Saul “enquired not of the LORD”
overlap.summary: 1 Samuel 28:6 says Saul enquired of the LORD and got no answer. 1 Chronicles 10:14 gives as a reason for his death that he “enquired not of the LORD”.
overlap.reasoning: In the KJV the same English verb is affirmed in Samuel and denied in Chronicles.
overlap.scope: The Hebrew uses two different verbs, “asked” in Samuel and “sought” in Chronicles, so the Hebrew does not affirm and deny the same word; 1 Chronicles 10:13 uses both verbs together for consulting the medium. Chronicles may mean that Saul did not seek the LORD in earnest or did not keep seeking. The contrast is clear in the KJV wording and weaker in the Hebrew. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text; a digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees.

overlap.title: What were the Urim and the Thummim, and how did they give an answer?
overlap.summary: Moses is told to put “the Urim and the Thummim” in the breastplate of judgment. Other items of the priest’s dress are described and their making commanded. Here the instruction is to put these in the breastplate: what they were, who made them, and how they gave judgment are not stated.
overlap.reasoning: The Urim and the Thummim are how the high priest bears “the judgment of the children of Israel”, and Numbers 27:21 makes them the means by which Joshua is to be told when to go out and come in. So they bear on how Israel is said to have received decisions from the Lord. Yet they appear with the definite article as if already known. The chapter gives the stones, the settings, the chains and the rings of the breastplate in detail, and commands that each be made; for the Urim and the Thummim it says only “put”. No passage read describes their material, their number, their maker, or what the priest did with them to get an answer.
overlap.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. That they were stones, or lots that were cast, or the twelve stones of the breastplate themselves, or that the answer came by light or by the priest’s own inspiration, are all readings; the checked passages state none of them, and this record asserts none. Check made for an answer elsewhere: every verse of the packaged KJV containing “Urim” or “Thummim” was read. There are seven, and all are quoted above. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible; passages that tell of enquiring of the Lord without using either word were not searched, and the check does not prove that no passage addresses the question. The Greek names are quoted because they are translations of the two words, where the KJV keeps the Hebrew words; no G is proposed, since a translated name beside a kept one is not a difference of statement. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

overlap.title: Complete conquest and continuing inhabitants
overlap.summary: Broad victory summaries in Joshua sit alongside explicit reports that many inhabitants remained.
overlap.reasoning: Joshua itself preserves an exception at Jerusalem, and Judges lists additional unconquered places. Totalizing military language need not mean every settlement was occupied or every person killed. This explicit exception qualifies an unqualified reading of destruction language; it does not by itself establish the historical extent of conquest or resolve the moral assessment of the killings.
overlap.scope: A literal exhaustive reading creates tension; a rhetorical summary of victory allows the stated exceptions. This does not independently date the conquest. Later presence can be explained by incomplete occupation or subsequent return, but these alternatives are not independently demonstrated here. The king list is not a population census or an archaeological chronology. These local accounts may narrate different stages or recap earlier events; their placement alone does not establish a dated sequence.

overlap.title: Joshua’s covenant assembly: Shechem or Shiloh?
overlap.summary: The KJV and the Hebrew set Joshua’s last assembly and covenant at Shechem. The Septuagint sets both at Shiloh, before the tent of God, and has no “sanctuary” in verse 26.
overlap.reasoning: The two text traditions name different towns for the same assembly. The Greek place agrees with where Joshua 18:1 puts the tabernacle; the Hebrew and KJV place a “sanctuary of the Lord” at Shechem without saying what it was.
overlap.scope: The passage does not say whether the “sanctuary” at Shechem was the tabernacle, a second holy place or something else, and it mentions no altar there. Do not claim the Greek is a deliberate correction or that the Hebrew is; neither is shown by these editions. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and neither edition settles which reading is earlier. English glosses in brackets are the researcher’s plain renderings, not lexicon entries.

overlap.title: At Gibeah Saul calls for “the ark of God”, or for the ephod?
overlap.summary: The KJV has Saul tell Ahiah to bring the ark of God. The Septuagint has him ask for the ephod, which Ahiah is said to wear in verse 3.
overlap.reasoning: The object Saul asks for is the ark in the KJV and Hebrew and the ephod in the Greek. The Greek matches verse 3, where the priest carries an ephod; the last place the KJV put the ark was Kirjathjearim (7:2).
overlap.scope: The KJV itself says the ark was with Israel at that time, so the ark could have been brought from Kirjathjearim; the KJV is not shown to be impossible. The difference recorded is the object named. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition, and the Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and neither edition settles which reading is earlier. English glosses in brackets are the researcher’s plain renderings, not lexicon entries.

overlap.title: The shewbread priest: Ahimelech, or Abiathar?
overlap.summary: 1 Samuel says David came to Ahimelech the priest for the bread, and that Abiathar was Ahimelech’s son. Mark 2:26 says it happened “in the days of Abiathar the high priest”.
overlap.reasoning: The priest who gives David the bread in 1 Samuel is Ahimelech; Mark names Abiathar, who in 1 Samuel is that priest’s son and escapes afterwards.
overlap.scope: The KJV matches the Greek of Mark here, so no G tag applies; this is a difference between Mark and 1 Samuel. Mark’s phrase could be read loosely as “in the lifetime of Abiathar, who was later high priest”, but 1 Samuel gives Ahimelech as the priest in office. Hebrew and Greek verse numbers in 1 Samuel 21 run one ahead of the KJV. The texts quoted are the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and a digital Textus Receptus; a digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees.

overlap.title: Who or what is “Shiloh” in Jacob’s blessing of Judah?
overlap.summary: Jacob says the sceptre shall not depart from Judah “until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be”. The verse does not say who or what Shiloh is. Everywhere else in the KJV Shiloh is a town, and Brenton’s Greek has no name here.
overlap.reasoning: The KJV prints Shiloh as a name and goes on “unto him”, so that Shiloh reads as someone who is to come. No person called Shiloh appears anywhere else in the packaged KJV: the word occurs in 30 other verses, from Joshua 18:1 to Jeremiah 41:5, and in each it is a place. Brenton’s Greek has no name at this point but a phrase, “the things laid up for him”. The verse sets a term to Judah’s sceptre, “until”, and does not say who or what marks that term.
overlap.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readers have taken Shiloh as a title of a ruler to come, as the town, or as a phrase meaning something like “that which is his” or “he whose it is”. Each is an interpretation; the verse states none of them, and this record asserts none. Ezekiel 21:27 has wording that some connect with the third reading; it does not mention Shiloh, Judah’s blessing or Genesis. Check made for an answer elsewhere: the packaged KJV was searched for “Shiloh” (31 verses; Joshua 16:6 has the separate name Taanathshiloh) and the list was read in shortened form; all but Genesis 49:10 concern the town (Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, Psalms 78:60, Jeremiah), and no New Testament verse contains the word. None explains Genesis 49:10. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible, and it does not prove that no passage addresses the question. The written and read spellings printed in the Hebrew edition are given for completeness only and are not the finding. The Greek is quoted because it bears on the question; this record proposes no G tag, and whether the Greek difference qualifies for one has not been examined here. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. overlap.title: What was the ephod Gideon made of the gold, and what did Israel do when it “went thither a whoring after it”?
overlap.summary: Gideon asks for the golden earrings of the spoil, makes “an ephod thereof” and puts it in his city, and all Israel goes “a whoring after it”. In the other verses compared an ephod is a thing a priest wears or brings. The passage does not say what Gideon’s ephod was, what it was for, or what the people did with it.
overlap.reasoning: In the verses compared outside Judges an ephod is listed among garments, is worn (“girded with a linen ephod”), or is brought by a priest when David wants to enquire. Gideon’s is made from the collected gold earrings, whose total weight is given as seventeen hundred shekels; the amount used in the ephod is not specified. It is “put” in a town, and draws “all Israel”. The passage gives the result, a snare to Gideon and his house, without saying what the object was or what the people did. That bears on what Gideon is being charged with, straight after he has said “the Lord shall rule over you”: making an idol, or setting up a means of enquiry or of priestly service away from the sanctuary.
overlap.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the passage states: that it was a priestly garment heavy with gold, kept at Ophrah and used to enquire of God; that it was an image, or the covering of an image, which the people worshipped; that it was a trophy of the victory that came to be treated as holy. Limits: the phrase “went a whoring after” is used six verses later of the Baalim, which shows the phrase can be used of other gods and does not show what was done at Ophrah; Micah’s ephod at Judges 17:5 stands beside teraphim in “an house of gods” and Hosea 3:4 lists an ephod with an image and teraphim, but being named together does not make the things alike; the weight given is that of the earrings asked for, and the verse does not say that all of it went into the ephod. Brenton’s Greek keeps the Hebrew word as a name at Judges 8:27 and has a Greek word for a shoulder-piece at Exodus 28:6; that is a difference within the Greek edition and settles nothing about the object. Check made: a whole-word search of the packaged KJV of Judges for “ephod” finds 8:27, 17:5, 18:14, 18:17, 18:18 and 18:20; the other verses quoted were chosen from a search of 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel and Hosea for the same word. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle what Gideon’s ephod was. No H or G is proposed. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. overlap.title: Jabesh Gilead and Saul's public legitimacy
overlap.summary: The rescue of Jabesh turns disputed kingship into public recognition; the same town later recovers Saul's body.
overlap.reasoning: Chapter 10 records both acclamation and dissent. Chapter 11 ends with a renewal of kingship after victory. Chapter 31's recovery of Saul's body supplies a later narrative connection to Jabesh.
overlap.scope: This is an inference about the narrative's structure, not independent confirmation of the battle, troop totals, or divine intervention.

overlap.title: Royal limits contrast with Solomon’s portrayal
overlap.summary: Deuteronomy limits royal accumulation; Kings portrays Solomon accumulating horses, wealth and wives.
overlap.reasoning: A prohibition and narrated disobedience are not contradictory factual reports. The heart-turning warning provides a close literary comparison.
overlap.scope: This does not independently verify the quantities, date the law or establish its enforcement.

overlap.title: A prohibition on returning to Egypt differs from a threatened return
overlap.summary: The king must not send people back to Egypt for horses; the covenant curse threatens return to Egypt.
overlap.reasoning: A prohibition does not guarantee that the forbidden or feared outcome cannot occur. The shared no-return wording creates tension if read as an unconditional prediction, but the statements have different functions.
overlap.scope: This does not identify a specific voyage, establish fulfillment or date the curse.
